newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian merchandise imports.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian merchandise imports.

text.p: Australian merchandise imports rose six percent in January, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported on Wednesday.
Market forecasts for the data had centred on a two percent rise, and ranged from a 1.0 percent fall to a 4.8 percent rise compared with 0.8 percent increase in December.
The following is a selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data.
NIGEL DOUGLAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH AUSTRALIA:

"Government expectations were for investment goods to rise by 17 percent this year. Obviously there's a lot of monthly volatility in these numbers, but that would be in line with the sort of thinking that's behind the government's forecasts."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"The big jump in capital goods is quite encouraging for a pick-up in business investment. This sort of figure would be consistent with a fairly marked deterioration in the balance of goods and services when those figures come out. We're looking at minus A$350-A$400 million in terms of the balance. The figure doesn't have any implications for monetary policy and no implications for the Australian dollar as well."
ANTHONY THOMPSON, HONG KONG BANK OF AUSTRALIA

"Overall, I think it's just another one of the indicators that we're going to get over early 1997 that'll add to the stock of stronger than expected numbers. It will continue to support the view that we're at the end of the rate cut cycle. I don't think the fact that they're much stronger than expected is necessarily bad for the long end of the bond market, because the good imports that we're getting on the capital goods side will, in the long run, add to productivity and therefore, help to keep a lid on inflationary pressures."

"It supports our view of firm economic growth led buy very strong business investment. The increase in imported vessels accounted for 2.3 percentage points of the 5.7 percent rise in merchandise imports. Stripping that out imports rose by around 3.5 percent."
DAVID BASSANESE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA

"It's basically this surge in capital imports. 29 percent is so large there must be some special factors involved there. But looking at the other indicators, the consumer component down one, consistent with reasoanbly weak spending at the consumer level, intermediate goods coming off as well, so I think we're going to have abstract from some special factors in there. The large rise, is it really indicative of the underlying strength of the economy?"
ANNETTE BEACHER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"The figures are unambiguously supportive for this business investment pick-up. But it has no implications for policy at all. We are all expecting this investment pick up, so it is just confirming what we already know."
